label: thm:ARformula
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:ARformula}
For $M,N \in \operatorname{mod}(A)$, we have
$$
\operatorname{Ext}_A^1(M,N) \cong D\overline{\operatorname{Hom}}_A(N,\tau_A(M))
\cong D\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_A(\tau_A^{-}(N),M).
$$
head: environment
name: Auslander, Reiten

label: thm:jacobian
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:jacobian}
Let $Q$ be a quiver, and let $\tilde{W}$ be a reduced hyperpotential
for $Q$.
Then the Jacobian algebra ${\mathcal P}(Q,\tilde{W})$
satisfies 
$$
E(M) = E^-(M)
$$
for all $M \in \operatorname{mod}({\mathcal P}(Q,\tilde{W}))$.

label: prop:introselfinjective
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:introselfinjective}
Let $A$ be selfinjective and $E$-symmetric.
We also assume that $A$ is connected and not semisimple.
Then for each simple $A$-module $S$ we have 
$$
\Omega_A^4(S) \cong \nu_A^{-1}(S).
$$
In particular, $A$ is twisted $4$-periodic.

title: Theorem
body_md:
For $M \in \operatorname{mod}(A)$, let
$$
P_1 \xrightarrow{f} P_0 \to M \to 0
$$
be a minimal projective presentation.
Then
the following are equivalent:
\begin{itemize}\itemsep2mm

\item[(i)]
$M$ is $\tau$-regular;

\item[(ii)]
$\operatorname{rk}(f) = r(P_1,P_0)$.

\end{itemize}

label: lem:pdim1stable
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:pdim1stable}
For $M,N \in \operatorname{mod}(A)$, the following hold:
If $\operatorname{proj.dim}(N) \le 1$, then
$$
\overline{\operatorname{Hom}}_A(M,\tau_A(N)) = \operatorname{Hom}_A(M,\tau_A(N)).
$$
head: environment

label: prop:hereditary2
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) $\implies$ (ii):
Let $P \in \operatorname{proj}(A)$, and let $U$ be an indecomposable submodule
of $P$.
Let $M := P$ and $N := \tau_A(U)$.
We get
\begin{align*}
E(M,N) &= \hom_A(N,\tau_A(M)) = 0,
\\
E^-(M,N) &= \hom_A(\tau_A^-(N),P) = 
\hom_A(\tau_A^-(\tau_A(U)),P). 
\end{align*}
Assuming (i) and keeping in mind that
$\hom_A(U,P) \not= 0$, it follows that $U$ must be projective.
This implies that $A$ is hereditary.

(ii) $\implies$ (i):
If $A$ is hereditary, then the Auslander-Reiten formula in
Theorem~\ref{thm:ARformula} combined with 
Lemma~\ref{lem:pdim1stable} and its dual
implies that (i) holds.
head: environment

label: prop:hereditary1
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We know already that (i) $\implies$ (ii) $\implies$ (iii)
for all algebras $A$.
The implication (iii) $\implies$ (iv) is part of
\cite[Corollary~1.8]{BS25} and relies on the assumption $\operatorname{gl.dim}(A) < \infty$.
Finally, (iv) $\implies$ (i) is a special case of
Proposition~\ref{prop:hereditary2}.

label: thm:monomial1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:monomial1}
Let $A = KQ/I$ be a monomial algebra, and let $R$ be the associated minimal
relation set.
Then the following are equivalent:
\begin{itemize}\itemsep2mm

\item[(i)]
$A$ is $1$-Iwanaga-Gorenstein;

\item[(ii)]
There is a disjoint union 
$$
Q_1 = Q_1' \cup \bigcup_{1 \le i \le q} Q_1^{(i)}
$$
such that for each $1 \le i \le q$
the arrows in $Q_1^{(i)}$ form a relation cycle $C_i$ for $A$ of length $|C_i| = |Q_1^{(i)}|$ and relation
length 
$$
r_i \ge 2,
$$ 
and
$$
R = \bigcup_{1 \le i \le q} \{ \text{relations associated to $C_i$}  \}. 
$$

\end{itemize}
head: environment
name: Lu--Zhu

label: cor:loops
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i): Since $\dim(A) < \infty$, we have $h^r = 0$ for some $r \ge 2$.
Now (i) follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:monomial1}(ii).

(ii):
Suppose there are loops $h_1 \not= h_2$ in $Q_1$ with
$s(h_1) = s(h_2)$.
Then Theorem~\ref{thm:monomial1}(ii) together with (i) implies that
$(h_2h_1)^l \notin I$ for all $l \ge 1$.
A contradiction, since $\dim(A) < \infty$.
head: environment

label: thm:monomial2
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:monomial2}
Let $A = KQ/I$ be a monomial algebra, and let $R$ be the associated minimal
relation set.
Then the following are equivalent:
\begin{itemize}\itemsep2mm

\item[(i)]
$A/AeA$ is $1$-Iwanaga-Gorenstein for each $e = e^2$ in $A$;

\item[(ii)]
There is a disjoint union 
$$
Q_1 = Q_1' \cup \bigcup_{1 \le i \le q} Q_1^{(i)}
$$
such that for each $1 \le i \le q$
the arrows in $Q_1^{(i)}$ form a relation cycle $C_i$ for $A$ of length $|C_i| = |Q_1^{(i)}|$ and relation
length 
$$
r_i \ge |C_i| - 1,
$$ 
and
$$
R = \bigcup_{1 \le i \le q} \{ \text{relations associated to $C_i$}  \}. 
$$

\end{itemize}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(ii) $\implies$ (i):
Assume that (ii) holds.
First, observe that (ii) implies that $A$ is $1$-Iwanaga-Gorenstein
by
Theorem~\ref{thm:monomial1}.
Now
pick a vertex $k$ of $Q$.
If $k \in \{ C_i \}_0$ for some relation cycle $C_i$ for $A$ of relation length $r_i$, then for each
relation $\rho$ associated to $C_i$ we have 
$k \in \{ \rho \}_0$.
(Here we use that $r_i \ge |C_i|-1$.)
Thus none of these relations is a path in the quiver of $A/Ae_kA$.
All relation cycles $C_j$ for $A$ with $k \notin \{C_j\}_0$ remain intact.
Thus their relations 
are the minimal relations for the monomial algebra $A/Ae_kA$.

Therefore $A/Ae_kA$ still satisfies condition (ii).
Now one can proceed by induction and gets that $A/AeA$ is $1$-Iwanaga-Gorenstein for all $e=e^2$ in $A$.

(i) $\implies$ (ii):
Assume that (i) holds.
Since $A$ is $1$-Iwanaga-Gorenstein, we get relation cycles for $A$ as described in Theorem~\ref{thm:monomial1}(ii).

Let $C = a_m \cdots a_2a_1$ be a relation cycle for $A$ of length $m \ge 1$ 
and relation length $r \ge 2$.
We have to show that $r \ge |C|-1$.

If there is a loop 
$h$ which belongs to $C$, then $C = h$, compare Corollary~\ref{cor:loops}(i).
In this case, we are done.

Thus, we can assume that $m \ge 2$ and that there are no loops belonging to  $C$.
Let $(D_t,\ldots,D_1)$ be a cycle decomposition of $C$.
Without loss of generality, we assume that 
$C = D_t \cdots D_2D_1$, $\min\{|D_t|,\ldots,|D_1|\} = |D_1|$ and that $D_1$ is multiplicity-free.
We can also assume that $D_1 = a_s \cdots a_2a_1$ and $s(a_i) = i$ for $1 \le i \le s$.
Thus $D_1$ looks as in Figure~\ref{fig:1}(1).

Claim 1: For each $1 \le i \le t$, we have $r \ge |D_i| - 1$.

Proof: Assume that $r \le |D_i|-2$ for some $i$.
Then there is a minimal relation $\rho \in R$ associated to
$C$ such that $1 \notin \{ \rho \}_0$.
Thus $\rho$ is still a minimal relation for $A/Ae_1A$.
However, since we removed $e_1$, we see that $\rho$ is no 
longer associated to a relation cycle for $A/Ae_1A$.
Thus by Theorem~\ref{thm:monomial1}, $A/Ae_1A$ is not $1$-Iwanaga-Gorenstein, a contradiction. $\square$

Claim 2: Let $t \ge 2$. Then we have $r \le |D_1|$. 

Proof: Let $t \ge 2$ and $r > |D_1|$. Then 
$(a_s \cdots a_2a_1)^l \notin I$ for all $l \ge 1$. A contradiction,
since $\dim(A) < \infty$. $\square$

Thus for $t \ge 2$, we have $r= s$ or $r = s-1$.

Claim 3: 
Let $t \ge 2$. 
Then for $2 \le i \le t$, we have
$\{ D_i \}_0 \subseteq \{ D_1 \}_0$.

Proof:
Since $|D_1| = s$ and $r \le s$, we know that
there is a subpath $\rho$ of $D_1$ such that
$\rho$ is a minimal relation for $A$.
Assume now that $k \in \{ D_i \}_0 \setminus \{ D_1 \}_0$.
Then $\rho$ does not run through $k$. 
Thus $\rho$ is still a minimal relation for $A/Ae_kA$.
However, 
$\rho$ is no 
longer associated to a relation cycle for $A/Ae_kA$.
Thus $A/Ae_kA$ is not $1$-Iwanaga-Gorenstein, a contradiction.
$\square$

Claim 4: 
We have $t=1$.

Proof:
Assume that $t \ge 2$, and let $D_i = b_{s_i} \cdots b_2b_1$. 
We know that there is no loop belonging to $C$.
Thus $|D_i| \ge |D_1| \ge 2$. 
We obviously have $s(a_1) = s(b_1)$.
We know from Claim 3 that $t(b_1) \in \{ 1,\ldots,s \}$.
Since there are no loops in $C$, we have $t(b_1) \not= 1$.
Assume that $t(b_1) \ge 3$. 
Thus the path $p := a_s \cdots a_{t(b_1)+1}a_{t(b_1)}$ has length at most $|D_1|-2$.
We know that $r \ge |D_i|-1$.
It follows that $(pb_1)^l \notin I$ for all $l \ge 1$.
A contradiction, since $\dim(A) < \infty$.
Thus we get $t(b_1) = t(a_1)$ and therefore $s(b_2) = s(a_2)$.
Analogously one shows now that $t(b_i) = t(a_i)$
for $2 \le i \le s$.
Thus we are in the situation of Figure~\ref{fig:1}(2).
We get
$(a_sb_{s-1} \cdots a_2b_1)^l \notin I$ for all $l \ge 1$,
a contradiction.
$\square$

We have shown that $C = D_1$
Combining this with Claim 1 yields that for each relation cycle
$C$ of relation length $r$, we have $r \ge |C|-1$.
This finishes the proof.
head: environment

label: cor:monomial2
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:monomial2}
Each relation cycle appearing in Theorem~\ref{thm:monomial2} is multiplicity-free.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: This is a consequence of the final paragraph of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:monomial2}(ii).
head: environment

label: thm:monomial3
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We know already from the introduction that
$$
\text{(i) $\implies$ (ii) $\implies$ (iii)}.
$$
By Theorem~\ref{thm:jacobian} we know also that (iv) $\implies$ (i).
We now assume that (iii) holds. We need to show that this implies (iv).

By \cite[Theorem~1.7]{BS25}, condition (iii) implies that $A/AeA$ is $1$-Iwanaga-Goren\-stein for each $e=e^2$ in $A$.
Thus we are in the situation of Theorem~\ref{thm:monomial2}(ii).

If all relation cycles $C_i$ have relation length $r_i = t_i|C_i| -1$
for some $t_i \ge 1$, then the associated relations form a
reduced hyperpotential $\tilde{W}$ for $Q$ and we get 
$A = KQ/I \cong {\mathcal P}(Q,\tilde{W})$.

Let $C = a_s \cdots a_2a_1$ be a relation cycle for $A$ of relation length
$r$.
We know from Theorem~\ref{thm:monomial2}(ii) 
and Corollary~\ref{cor:monomial2} that 
$C$ is multiplicity-free and that 
$$
r \ge s-1.
$$
We illustrate $C$ in Figure~\ref{fig:1}(1).
We assume now without loss of generality that 
$s(a_1),\ldots,s(a_s)$ are the only vertices of $Q$, and that $s(a_i) = i$
for $1 \le i \le s$.
Here we use Corollary~\ref{cor:reduction4}.

If $r = s-1$, then we are done, since the relations associated to $C$ will be part of a hyperpotential $\tilde{W}$.

Thus, we assume from now on that 
$$
r \ge s.
$$

Claim 1: There is no $b \in Q_1$ with
$s(b) \not= t(b)$ and
$b \not= a_i$ for all $1 \le i \le s$.


Proof:
Assume there is such an arrow $b$. Without loss of generality, let
$s(b) = 1$ and $t(b) = i \not= 1$.
This is illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:2}(1).
Then $(a_s \cdots a_{i+1}a_ib)^l \notin I$ for all $l \ge 1$. 
A contradiction, since $\dim(A) < \infty$. $\square$

Claim 2:
$Q$ has at most one loop.

Proof:
By Corollary~\ref{cor:loops}(ii), there is at most one loop at each vertex of $Q$.
Next, suppose that $Q$ has two different loops $h_1$ and $h_2$.
Without loss of generality let $s(h_1) = 1$ and $s(h_2) = i \not= 1$.
We illustrated this in Figure~\ref{fig:2}(2).
Then $
(a_s \cdots a_ih_ia_{i-1} \cdots a_1h_1)^l \notin I$ for all $l \ge 1$. 
A contradiction, since $\dim(A) < \infty$. $\square$

Claim 3: $Q$ has no loop.

Proof: Assume that $Q$ has exactly one loop $h$.
Without loss of generality, let $s(h) = 1$.
This situation is illustrated in Figure~\ref{fig:2}(3).
If $r > s$, then $(a_s \cdots a_2a_1h)^l \notin I$ for all $l \ge 1$.
A contradiction, since $\dim(A) < \infty$. 
Thus $r=s$.
There is a minimal relation $h^p \in R$ for some $p \ge 2$.
Let $M$ be the uniserial string module
$$
M = M(a_{s-1} \cdots a_2a_1h^{p-1}).
$$
Note that $\underline{\dim}(M) = (p,1,\ldots,1)$.
Then we have $E(M) = 0$ and $E^-(M) = p-1 \not= 0$.
This is easily calculated by computing the minimal projective presentation 
$$
P(2)^{p-1} \to P(1) \to M \to 0
$$
and the minimal injective presentation 
$$
0 \to M \to I(s) \to I(s)^{p-1}
$$
of $M$.
This gives us the $g$-vectors 
$g(M) = (-1,p-1,0\ldots,0)$ and $g^-(M) = (0,\ldots,0,p-2)$, respectively.
Then one uses the well known formulas
\begin{align*}
E(M) &= \dim \operatorname{End}_A(M) + \langle g(M),\underline{\dim}(M)\rangle,
\\
E^-(M) &= \dim \operatorname{End}_A(M) + \langle g^-(M),\underline{\dim}(M)\rangle.
\end{align*}
Thus the irreducible component
$$
{\mathcal Z} := \overline{{\mathcal O}_M}
$$
in generically $\tau$-regular but not $\tau^-$-regular.
This proves that $\operatorname{Irr}^\tau(A) \not= \operatorname{Irr}^{\tau^-}(A)$,
a contradiction. $\square$

Claim 4: 
We have $r = ts-1$ for some $t \ge 2$.

Proof:
We know by Claims 1 and 3 that the only arrows of $Q$ are $a_1,\ldots,a_s$. 
Thus $A$ is a cyclic Nakayama algebra.
Then the claim follows from
\cite[Proposition~1.10]{BS25}. $\square$

This finishes the proof.

label: thm:GSS

head: environment
name: Green, Snashall, Solberg

label: lem:stablehom
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:stablehom}
Let $A$ be selfinjective, and let $S$ be a simple and non-projective 
$A$-module.
Then for each $M \in \operatorname{mod}(A)$, we have
$$
\operatorname{Hom}_A(S,\tau_A(M)) = \underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_A(S,\tau_A(M)).
$$
head: environment

label: prop:selfinjective
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i):
Assume that $S$ and $T$ are simple $A$-modules.
Then they are non-projective, since $A$ is connected and not semisimple. In particular $\tau_A^m(S) \not= 0$ for all $m \in \mathbb{Z}$.

Let $P := P(T)$ and $M := P \oplus \tau_A(S)$.
Note that $\nu_A^{-1}(T) \cong \operatorname{soc}(P)$.
Then
$$
\tau_A(M) \cong \tau_A^2(S) 
\text{\quad and \quad}
\tau_A^-(M) \cong S.
$$
We get
\begin{align*} E(M) =
\hom_A(M,\tau_A(M)) &= [\tau_A^2(S):T] + 
\hom_A(\tau_A(S),\tau_A^2(S))
\\
&\ge  [\tau_A^2(S):T] + \dim \overline{\operatorname{Hom}}_A(\tau_A(S),\tau_A^2(S))
\\
&= [\tau_A^2(S):T] + \dim \underline{\operatorname{Hom}}_A(S,\tau_A(S))
\\
&= [\tau_A^2(S):T] + \hom_A(S,\tau_A(S)).
\end{align*}
(For the last equality, we used Lemma~\ref{lem:stablehom}.)
Furthermore, we have
$$
E^-(M) = \hom_A(\tau_A^-(M),M) = \hom_A(S,P) + \hom_A(S,\tau_A(S)). 
$$
Note that
$$
\hom_A(S,P) =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if $S \cong \nu_A^{-1}(T)$},
\\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}.
$$
Since $E(M) = E^-(M)$,
we get 
$$
\hom_A(S,P) \ge [\tau_A^2(S):T].
$$
Therefore
$$
[\tau_A^2(S):T] =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if $S \cong \nu_A^{-1}(T)$},
\\
0 & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}.
$$
(We used here that $\tau_A^2(S) \not= 0$.)
Thus $\tau_A^2(S) \cong \nu_A(S)$.

(ii):
Since $A$ is selfinjective,
we have functorial isomorphisms
$$
\tau_A \cong \Omega_A^2 \circ \nu_A \cong \nu_A \circ \Omega_A^2\colon
\underline{\operatorname{mod}}(A) \to \underline{\operatorname{mod}}(A).
$$
Thus the condition $\tau_A^2(S) \cong \nu_A(S)$ is equivalent to $\Omega_A^4(S) \cong \nu_A^{-1}(S)$.
Now Theorem~\ref{thm:GSS} says that $A$ is twisted $4$-periodic.
head: environment
